Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because the narrative spans an entire academic year (from autumn to the following autumn), the writer effectively uses summary and exposition to compress time, introduce the ensemble of characters, and provide the narrator's retrospective reflections. At the same time, the writer slows the pace down to dramatize the most emotionally pivotal moments as real-time scenes with dialogue and action—such as the kiss at the bus stop, the midnight conversations with Johan in the kitchen, the breakup with Carl, and the final confrontation with Lizzy. This careful alternation allows the story to cover a long period of personal growth while remaining vivid, grounded, and emotionally engaging.
